description:
The golden corpus for the jwks.v1 wire contract. This manifest is the SINGLE inventory of the corpus: the Go runner and the Python runner both read THIS file over THESE fixtures, so a third copy of the list cannot drift out of step with the first two (G-70).

The consumer named throughout is dev-health-go's the `Keys()` method of dev-health-go's `Ed25519JWKSVerifier`, which is what actually reads this document in production. The Go runner drives the REAL consumer against every fixture, so `accept` means "the consumer accepts it" as well as "the schema validates it" -- the two directions that together stop the schema drifting either looser or stricter than the code it describes.

accept.why: The ordinary steady state: one key, `use` omitted. The minimal document the consumer accepts.
`use` present and `sig`. Means exactly what its absence means; both forms are on the wire today because the producer emits it and the consumer does not require it.
A rotation in progress. Two DISTINCT kids, so envelopes signed by the outgoing key still verify while they remain within their TTL. This is why `keys` is an array and not an object.
`kid` at exactly the consumer's 256-byte ceiling. An upper bound with no at-the-bound case is a bound nobody has checked: a future off-by-one to 255 would break no other fixture.

reject.why: No `keys` at all. The consumer decodes to a nil slice and refuses on len==0, so the schema must not treat the member as optional.

A syntactically valid document that yields no key material. The consumer refuses it rather than reporting a healthy-but-empty keyset -- otherwise every verification fails as a kid lookup miss, which is indistinguishable from an unknown kid and sends the reader to the wrong cause.

An extra top-level member. The consumer decodes with DisallowUnknownFields and rejects the WHOLE document, so a plausible-looking addition like `issuer` is not forward-compatible here -- it is an outage.

A standard RFC 7517 member the consumer does not know. RFC 7517 says ignore unrecognised JWK members; the consumer refuses them. The schema follows the CONSUMER, because a schema that permitted `x5c` would certify a document that cannot be read.

The private scalar in a document whose entire purpose is to publish the PUBLIC half. Refused by `additionalProperties` rather than by a rule naming `d`: the subtractive contract makes the leak unrepresentable instead of prohibited, so `p`, `q` and every other private member are closed by the same clause without being enumerated.
Wrong key type. Refused before any key material is looked at.
The same key TYPE (OKP) on the key-agreement curve. X25519 never signs anything, so accepting it here would defer a certain failure to a confusing signature mismatch later.

`alg` is optional in RFC 7517 and REQUIRED here, because the consumer compares it literally -- an absent `alg` reads as the empty string and the document is refused. The schema states the requirement rather than letting it surface as a mystery rejection.
Case matters. The consumer's comparison is byte equality, not a case-folded match.
An encryption key offered where a signing key is required.
No `kid`. The consumer reads the missing member as "", which fails its non-empty check, and an envelope could never be matched to this key anyway.

An empty `kid`. Refused by the pattern rather than by `minLength`, so that this case and the whitespace-only case below trip the SAME keyword -- they are one rule in the consumer (TrimSpace then non-empty) and are kept one rule here.

A `kid` of three spaces. `minLength: 1` ACCEPTS this -- length 3 -- and the consumer REFUSES it, because it trims before testing for empty. Excluding space from the alphabet is what closes the gap; executed against the consumer's own validKeyID, not argued.

256 code points and 512 UTF-8 BYTES. `maxLength: 256` accepts it and the consumer refuses it, because JSON Schema counts code points and Go's len() counts bytes. Restricting the alphabet to one-byte characters makes the two counts the same number; this fixture is what fails if someone "simplifies" the pattern back to a maxLength.
One character past the consumer's ceiling. Paired with valid-kid-at-maximum-length.json so the boundary is pinned from both sides.
No key material.

Padded base64url. RFC 7515 section 2 forbids the padding, the consumer's RawURLEncoding rejects `=`, and Python's urlsafe_b64decode ACCEPTS it -- so a Python-side reader written later would disagree with the consumer unless the wire form is pinned here.

The standard base64 alphabet. `+` and `/` are rejected by the consumer's RawURLEncoding and silently ACCEPTED by Python's urlsafe_b64decode, which translates them before decoding. Same split as the padding case, different cause.

42 characters, which decodes to 31 bytes. BOTH base64 decoders accept it happily -- the length is not checked anywhere in the decode. ed25519.Verify PANICS on a 31-byte public key rather than returning an error, BUT THE CONSUMER GUARDS THIS ITSELF: Keys() compares the decoded length against ed25519.PublicKeySize before returning a key, so the panic is not reachable through it. An earlier version of this note called the schema the only guard -- false, and written after reading the very function that disproves it. The pattern is defence-in-depth and a statement of the wire form, not the thing preventing a crash.

44 characters, which decodes to 33 bytes. Same panic class as the short case; kept as its own fixture because a bound checked on one side only is not a bound. The consumer already refuses both lengths; see the short-case entry for the sole-guard claim that was corrected.

reject_by_client.why: Two keys sharing one `kid` and carrying DIFFERENT key material. The schema accepts it and the consumer refuses it. `uniqueItems` cannot help: it compares whole array items, and these items differ in `x`, so they are unique by that test while being ambiguous by the only measure that matters -- which key does an envelope stamped with this kid verify against? Executed both directions rather than reasoned.

reject_by_client_note: Valid against the schema, refused by the consumer. The category exists for rules JSON Schema cannot express at all, never for rules that were merely inconvenient to write.
regex_dialect_note: Both patterns here use explicit character RANGES and no shorthand class. `\d`, `\w`, `\s` and `\b` are Unicode-aware in Python's re and ASCII-only in RE2 and ECMA-262, which is the split that has bitten the other surfaces in this directory; `[!-~]` and `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` mean the same thing in all three.
known_gap_duplicate_json_members:
A repeated JSON member inside one key object -- two `kid` members, say -- is NOT refused by any current reader. Every parser keeps the LAST value, so the earlier one never reaches validation. error.v1 refuses this at the raw-bytes boundary before decoding, but that check lives in a client this repository owns; the JWKS consumer is dev-health-go, and adding a shadow reader here to catch it would create exactly the second implementation this programme exists to remove. Recorded as a gap for a dev-health-go change, not papered over with a local wrapper.

FILED AS CHAOS-4951 (dev-health-go: refuse duplicate JSON members in a JWKS before decode, raw-text red-first fixture, positive control, no reliance on last-wins).

narrower_than_consumer.why:
Go's encoding/json matches struct field names CASE-INSENSITIVELY, and DisallowUnknownFields compares AFTER that match -- so the consumer reads {"KEYS":[{"KTY":...}]} as an ordinary document and accepts it. The schema refuses it.

WHY THE SCHEMA REFUSES IT, corrected after round 2 falsified the first reason given. That reason was "admitting any casing would make additionalProperties:false unenforceable", and it is FALSE -- executed: a schema declaring both `keys` and `KEYS` still rejects an undeclared `issuer` by additionalProperties. The keyword keeps working.

The true reason is that JSON Schema matches property names EXACTLY, so admitting case variants means ENUMERATING them: every casing of every member in `properties`, and `required` rewritten as a disjunction over all of them. That is combinatorial in the number of members and it leaves the wire form with no canonical spelling for a producer to target. Refusing is not a limitation of the keyword; it is a choice to have one spelling.
JSON null decodes into Go's string field as the zero value, so the consumer sees an empty use and accepts it. const:sig refuses null. Absence is how this contract says nothing.

The consumer TrimSpaces before testing for empty, so a padded kid trims to something non-empty and is accepted -- and an envelope's kid header would then have to match the UNTRIMMED value to resolve, a silent mismatch waiting to happen. The schema refuses the padding outright.

unicode.IsSpace(NUL) is FALSE, so TrimSpace does not strip it and the consumer accepts a kid carrying an embedded NUL. The schema's printable-ASCII class refuses it. Stored as a JSON backslash-u-0000 escape, the only way a NUL can appear in a JSON document.

The consumer's test is `use != "" && use != "sig"`, so an EMPTY use is tolerated alongside sig; `const: sig` refuses it. Absence is how this contract says nothing, and a field present-and-blank carries no information its omission does not.

THIS FIXTURE EXISTS BECAUSE ITS ABSENCE WAS THE ROUND-2 BLOCK. The narrowing was named in the schema description and exempted by a predicate in the differential harness, and had no fixture asserting both halves -- so it was a SENTENCE, in the very commit whose message was that narrowings must stop being sentences. Round 1 blocked this contract for four prose-only narrowings; round 2 blocked it for a fifth, added while fixing the first four.

narrower_than_consumer_note:
THE CATEGORY THIS CORPUS WAS MISSING, added after codex round 1 blocked the first version.

These documents are ACCEPTED by the real consumer and REFUSED by the schema. Each is a deliberate narrowing, and each is here because the first version STATED its narrowings in prose and got the list wrong: it declared two, and there were five.

They cannot be reject entries. TestRejectedJWKSFixturesAreAlsoRefusedByTheRealConsumer asserts every reject fixture is refused by the consumer too -- the check that stops the schema drifting stricter than the code it describes. Filing a narrowing there would force that test to be weakened, and it is the most valuable test in the file.

WHY PROSE WAS NOT ENOUGH, stated plainly because it is the lesson: that test PASSED on the blocked version. It passed because not one of the 20 reject fixtures happened to exercise any undeclared narrowing. A correct instrument fed a corpus that cannot trip it reports coverage it does not have. Each row below turns one sentence of prose into an assertion executed in both directions.

ROUND 2 BLOCKED THIS CATEGORY FOR BEING INCOMPLETE, which is the round-1 defect committed inside its own fix. `use: ""` was listed in the schema description and exempted by a harness predicate, and had no fixture. A predicate without a fixture is worse than prose alone: prose merely fails to test the narrowing, while a predicate actively EXCUSES the disagreement, so the differential stays green over an asymmetry nothing asserts. The invariant is now enforced mechanically -- every predicate must have a fixture and every predicate must be exercised -- rather than by remembering to add both.
known_gap_trailing_content:
A mounted JWKS may carry a SECOND JSON value after a valid document and the consumer silently ignores it: Keys() decodes with a streaming json.Decoder, which reads exactly one value and never inspects the remainder. Executed -- a valid document followed by null, and a file holding two whole JWKS documents, are BOTH accepted, yielding only the first document's keys.

This corpus cannot express it: every fixture here is a single JSON document and the schema never sees bytes. Not hypothetical for rotation either -- cmd/query-api's CheckJWKS carries a comment describing exactly this, where a two-document file with kid old then kid new makes verification fail on new while a naive health check reports the instance healthy. Found by codex round 1. FOLDED INTO CHAOS-4951, which CF retitled to cover the raw-bytes boundary as a whole -- refuse duplicate members AND trailing content before decode, requiring EOF after the single document. The case-insensitive field match and the use:null acceptance are recorded there too, as a decision the Go fix must make explicitly: refuse, or document with a test. One ticket, one manifest reference.
differential_harness_note:
The fixture lists below are NOT the whole check. TestTheSchemaAndTheRealConsumerAgreeExceptOnDeclaredNarrowings generates 2000 documents by mutating a valid baseline and asserts the schema and the real consumer reach the same verdict, except where a declared narrowing or a client-enforced rule explains the difference. Both exemption lists are PREDICATES in that file, so a new member of a known class passes and a genuinely new class fails.

It exists because the hand-written corpus could not catch what round 1 caught: a corpus contains only the cases someone thought of, and the test policing that direction was green while four narrowings went undeclared. Borrowed from lane-auth-wave1, who built the same shape with PostgreSQL as the oracle after their own corpus missed a case for the identical reason.

Mutation-proven in both directions, each with the mutation itself verified as applied: deleting the case-insensitivity predicate reports 148 undeclared narrowings; widening the x pattern to admit a 42-character key reports documents the consumer refuses. The first attempt at the former was a silent no-op -- the edit did not match after formatting -- and a mutation control that did not mutate proves nothing, so the applied change is now asserted before the run.
